A fiscal sponsor is a tax-exempt organization that lets a project receive grants and tax-deductible donations without forming its own non-profit. Details below were checked in August 2026 and change; confirm with each sponsor.

<span id="the-two-models"></span>
== The two models ==

{| class="wikitable"
|-
!
! Model A (comprehensive)
! Model C (pre-approved grant)
|-
| '''Legal status of your project'''
| Becomes a program of the sponsor
| Stays a separate entity or group
|-
| '''Who holds the money'''
| The sponsor, on your behalf
| You, after the sponsor grants it to you
|-
| '''Who is responsible'''
| The sponsor carries legal and financial responsibility and oversees the project
| You carry most responsibility; the sponsor reviews the grant
|-
| '''Fit'''
| Groups that want the sponsor to handle operations: payroll, contracts, insurance, compliance
| Projects with a specific funder who has agreed to give, and that already run themselves
|-
| '''Cost'''
| Usually a percentage fee on money received; commonly cited ranges are around 5 to 15 percent, set by each sponsor
| Usually a fee on each grant, plus the sponsor’s review
|}

<span id="questions-to-ask-any-sponsor"></span>
== Questions to ask any sponsor ==

* Which model do you offer, and what fee do you charge on what?
* Do you accept software and open source projects?
* Is there a funding precondition? Some Model C programs, for example Tides Center’s, required committed funding of roughly 50,000 to 100,000 US dollars before submission when last checked.
* What happens if a campaign or advocacy opportunity comes up while we are sponsored? (This matters most under Model A.)
* Who owns the code and the brand if we leave?
* How long does onboarding take, and what is the notice to leave?

<span id="things-to-know-when-choosing"></span>
== Things to know when choosing ==

* '''Tax status matters.''' A 501(c)(3) sponsor can receive tax-deductible donations and foundation grants. A 501(c)(6) cannot. Open Source Collective, for example, is a 501(c)(6), so donations to it are not tax-deductible, and many foundation grants require a 501(c)(3) grantee.
* '''Check the sponsor still exists.''' Open Collective Foundation dissolved at the end of 2024.
* '''Candidates for open source projects:''' Software Freedom Conservancy is a long-standing sponsor of free and open source projects. Directories such as TSNE’s fiscal-sponsor directory list hundreds of others; screen by model, fee and mission fit.
